lesson.title: The Waveform's Baseline: Finding the DC Component
lesson.summary: The DC component of a signal is its average value over one period, the constant a0 term of the Fourier series that would remain if every AC harmonic were filtered away.
lesson.body:
For any periodic voltage or current, the DC component answers a simple question: if you averaged this signal out over time, what steady, constant value would be left? That is precisely the Average Value prerequisite, now placed inside the Fourier series framework as the single term with zero frequency, a0 = (1/T) times the integral of f(t) over one period. In the full series f(t) = a0 + the sum of [an cos(n omega0 t) + bn sin(n omega0 t)], a0 is the only piece that does not oscillate; every cosine and sine term averages to exactly zero over a full period on its own, so when you average the whole signal, only a0 survives.

This has a very physical meaning. A true averaging DC voltmeter reads exactly a0 and nothing else. A series coupling capacitor is specifically designed to block a0 while letting every oscillating term pass through, which is the subject of the next chapter. In a Fourier series, a0 is a single fixed number, not a function of time, unlike every other term in the series.

Here is a fully worked example drawn straight from digital and power electronics: a pulse waveform, or PWM signal, that sits at 5 V for the first 2 ms of a 10 ms period and at 0 V for the remaining 8 ms, a 20 percent duty cycle. Its DC component is a0 = (1/T) times the integral of v(t) over one period = (1/10 ms)[5 V times 2 ms + 0 V times 8 ms] = (1/10)(10) = 1 V. Notice this equals duty cycle times amplitude (0.20 times 5 V = 1 V), which is exactly the operating principle behind PWM based dimmers and digital to analog converters: after low pass filtering removes the switching harmonics, changing the duty cycle directly changes the resulting DC level.

A second short check ties this back to the previous chapter. The full-wave rectified sine wave was shown to have a0 = 2A/pi, about 0.637A, a nonzero DC component, while the odd and half-wave symmetric square wave used throughout earlier chapters has a0 = 0 exactly. That is not a coincidence: it directly confirms the general rule proved in the Half-Wave Symmetry chapter, that any waveform with half-wave symmetry must have zero DC component, and any waveform without it is free to have a nonzero one. Whether a signal's DC component turns out to be positive, negative, or zero, it is always a single fixed number describing where the waveform is centered, which sets up a clean contrast with the AC component covered next, the part of the signal that actually moves.
